content: Thalassaemia is a genetic disorder characterized by a quantitative abnormality in haemoglobin production, caused by mutations in the genes responsible for alpha or beta globin synthesis. The imbalance in globin chain production leads to unpaired globin chains, which cause damage to cell membranes and result in cell death within various organ systems. Additionally, the destruction of erythroid precursors in the bone marrow leads to haemolytic anaemia. Managing the systemic health effects of thalassaemia is a lifelong challenge, and failure to address associated dental and orthodontic complications can significantly increase the public health, financial, and personal burden of the disease. Currently, there is a lack of evidence-based guidelines to assist healthcare providers and patients in managing the dental and orthodontic complications associated with thalassaemia. This review aimed to evaluate the available evidence on treatment methods for these complications to inform future clinical recommendations. It serves as an update to a Cochrane Review initially published in 2019. The objective of this review was to assess the effectiveness of various treatment methods for dental and orthodontic complications in individuals with thalassaemia. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted in September 2022 using the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis and Genetic Disorders Group's Haemoglobinopathies Trials Register, as well as nine additional online databases and trial registries in January 2022. Reference lists of relevant articles and reviews were also examined, and experts in haematology, dentistry, and related fields were contacted, along with pharmaceutical companies and researchers. The review focused on identifying randomised controlled trials (RCTs), both published and unpublished, that evaluated treatments for dental and orthodontic complications in individuals diagnosed with thalassaemia, regardless of phenotype, severity, age, sex, or ethnic background. Two independent reviewers screened 37,242 titles retrieved from the search. After removing duplicates, two potentially relevant RCTs were identified. Upon further assessment, one study was excluded, and the other was included in the review. The included study was a parallel-design RCT conducted in Saudi Arabia, involving 29 participants (19 males and 10 females) with thalassaemia. The average age of participants was approximately 23 years. The study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of photodynamic therapy as an adjunct to conventional full-mouth ultrasonic scaling in the treatment of gingivitis. The results provided very low-certainty evidence suggesting that the combination of full-mouth ultrasonic scaling and photodynamic therapy may improve gingival index scores and reduce bleeding on probing after 12 weeks, compared to full-mouth ultrasonic scaling alone. No other studies were identified that assessed interventions for the broader range of dental or orthodontic complications associated with thalassaemia. The included study had several limitations, including an unclear risk of bias, a short follow-up period, and a lack of data on safety or adverse effects. As a result, the evidence is insufficient to make definitive clinical recommendations. The authors concluded that while the included study showed a greater reduction in gingivitis with the addition of photodynamic therapy, the evidence is of very low certainty. Future research is needed to address the gaps in knowledge. High-quality RCTs are essential to evaluate the effectiveness of various treatment modalities for dental and orthodontic complications in individuals with thalassaemia. It is also critical for future studies to assess the safety and potential adverse effects of these interventions.
